caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Cameroon's debt was reset by HIPC/MDRI relief in 2006, falling from 17.6% of GDP to 11.2% by 2008, the series low. The government then borrowed steadily to fund infrastructure (dams, roads, the 2019 AFCON stadiums), and the 2014 oil crash plus Boko Haram security costs accelerated the climb: debt reached 47.2% of GDP in 2021, the series high, before easing to a projected 40.3% in 2025. Borrowing is a mix of concessional, Chinese bilateral, and Eurobond issuance. The CEMAC regional ceiling and IMF program surveillance have imposed some discipline, but debt has still roughly quadrupled from its post-HIPC low, and servicing costs are rising as concessional access shrinks.
inflation_management: Cameroon's inflation is anchored by the Central African CFA franc's peg to the euro and the BEAC regional central bank, which kept price growth low through most of the period: inflation averaged under 3% from 2009 to 2021, with a low of 0.6% in 2017. The 2008 food-fuel crisis (5.3%) and the 2022 global shock (6.3%) were the main breaches, with inflation peaking at 7.4% in 2023 before easing to 4.5% in 2024 and a projected 3.4% in 2025. The peg has delivered stability but at the cost of an independent monetary policy; when the Anglophone crisis and oil shocks hit, adjustment fell entirely on fiscal policy.

key_events.event: HIPC completion-point relief cut debt to 11.2% of GDP, the series low.
Oil price crash and Boko Haram insurgency in the Far North raised security spending and cut revenues.
Anglophone crisis escalated into armed conflict in the Northwest and Southwest, disrupting agriculture and trade.
Paul Biya won a seventh term (2018); the 2019 AFCON hosting was stripped over stadium delays.
COVID-19 pushed debt to 44.7%; an IMF program supported the response.
October 2025 presidential election returned the 92-year-old Biya for another term amid opposition claims of fraud.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued low inflation under the CFA peg with moderate growth, but debt is on a structurally rising path and the succession question around Biya (in power since 1982) is the dominant uncertainty. Upside comes from oil and gas projects and regional trade; downside is a disorderly political transition or renewed conflict. Uncertainty is moderate-to-high and heavily political rather than macroeconomic.
